note: This greeting uses the plural días, even when greeting one person.
Buenas agrees with the feminine plural noun tardes.
Buenas noches can also mean ‘good night’ when saying goodbye.
A common short greeting when you meet someone for the first time.
Hasta means ‘until’; mañana means ‘tomorrow’ here.
Usted is a respectful form of singular you. Está agrees with usted.
Estoy means ‘I am’; the subject yo is usually unnecessary.
Me permite + infinitive is a courteous way to ask permission; le and su refer to usted here.
Me llamo literally means ‘I call myself.’

en: May I ask where you are from?
note: De dónde asks about origin. Me permite preguntarle makes the question respectful.
Use ser + de to say where someone is from.
Podría + infinitive makes a polite request. Here podría addresses usted.
Podría and por favor make this a courteous request to repeat something.
Put no before the verb to make a negative statement.
Esta agrees with the feminine noun palabra; qué asks ‘what.’

en: How do you say this in Spanish?
note: Se dice means ‘one says’ or ‘it is said’; esto means ‘this.’
Hablo is the yo form of hablar; un poco de means ‘a little.’
Tengo is the irregular yo form of tener, ‘to have.’
Con permiso politely asks to pass; puedo + infinitive means ‘I can.’
Muchas agrees with the feminine plural noun gracias.
A standard response to gracias; literally ‘for nothing.’
Lo refers to what you are sorry about; siento comes from sentir.
Podría + infinitive makes a polite request to usted. Ayudarme means to help me.
Un is masculine because momento is a masculine noun.

en: Could I have some water, please?
es: ¿Me da un poco de agua, por favor?
note: Me da... por favor is a common courteous request. Da is the usted form of dar.
Spanish uses tener here: literally ‘I have hunger.’
Spanish uses tener here: literally ‘I have thirst.’

en: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?
note: Disculpe politely gets attention. Dónde asks where; está indicates location.

en: Excuse me, how much does this cost?
note: Disculpe politely gets attention. Cuánto asks about the price.
Quisiera is a common polite way to say ‘I would like.’
La cuenta is the bill or check at a restaurant.

en: May I pay by card, please?
note: Puedo + infinitive asks permission. Con tarjeta means by card.
Estoy + gerund describes what is happening now. Gracias keeps the response courteous.

en: Do you have a smaller size, please?
es: ¿Tiene una talla más pequeña, por favor?
note: Tiene addresses usted. Más pequeña means smaller.

en: I'd like to try on this shirt, please.
es: Quisiera probarme esta camisa, por favor.
note: Quisiera is a polite request. Probarse means to try on clothing.

en: Excuse me, where is the bus stop?
es: Disculpe, ¿dónde está la parada del autobús?
note: Disculpe politely gets attention. Del is the contraction of de + el.

es: Un boleto al centro, por favor.
note: Al combines a + el; al centro means ‘to the city center.’

en: Does this bus go to the airport?
note: Va is a form of ir, ‘to go’; este agrees with autobús.

en: Could you tell me how to get to the hotel?
note: Podría decirme is a courteous request. Cómo llegar means how to get there.
A male speaker says perdido; a female speaker says perdida.

es: Gire a la derecha, por favor.
note: Gire is a formal usted command. A la derecha means to the right.
Siga is the formal usted command from seguir. Derecho means straight ahead here.
Reservación is common in Latin America; reserva is also widely used.
Hay asks whether something exists; aquí means ‘here.’

en: Excuse me, what time is it?
note: Disculpe adds politeness. Qué hora es asks for the current time.
A qué hora asks ‘at what time’; abren addresses a business or its staff.
No encuentro naturally means ‘I can't find’; mi means ‘my.’

es: Por favor, llame a un médico.
note: Llame is the formal usted command from llamar. The a comes before a person.
Todo means ‘everything’ and takes a singular verb here.
Que tenga is a courteous wish addressed to usted.
